pr_title: Execute EnrichPolicyRunner on a non dedicated master node.
pr_body:
In case a cluster consists out of multiple nodes then delegate the execution of EnrichPolicyRunner
to a node that is not the elected master and nodes that are not dedicated master.

Closes #70436

issue_context.title: Enrich policy execution can be a heavy burden on the master
issue_context.body:
Today when an enrich policy is executed, building a new copy of the enrich index, we use the elected master to coordinate the underlying reindex task which operates in batches of 10,000 documents by default. A user reported that a particular enrich policy execution would reliably cause their master to fail with an `OutOfMemoryError`. The policy in question was of `geo_match` type and the documents, containing geoshapes, could be quite large. Their master had a 1GB heap, which is appropriate for their small and well-run cluster, but it appears it simply could not hold 10,000 geoshapes in memory on the master at once.

As a workaround they reduced the (undocumented?) `enrich.fetch_size` to 5000, which was enough to avoid the OOM, but I'm still concerned about the strain this puts on the master.

A few ideas for possible improvements:

- Move the coordination of the reindexing job onto a different node.
- Strengthen a circuit-breaker to prevent an OOM like this one.
- Adapt the reindex batch size to the resources available.

I think we should definitely do the first; the other two are harder.

See https://discuss.elastic.co/t/why-does-an-enrich-policy-get-executed-on-the-master-node/263241 for more details.

/cc @consulthys
comments:
Thanks for filing this bug @DaveCTurner and @consulthys for reporting this problem in the forum. I think we have underestimated the resources it takes to rebuild the policy index with geo shapes.

> Move the coordination of the reindexing job onto a different node.

Yes, I think we should migrate the enrich policy execution to use the persistent task framework, so that these operations (for any policy type) get executed on other nodes (anything but master nodes).

Instead of migrating the enrich policy execution over to persistent tasks, the enrich policy execution can be refactored that just perform the execution policy on another non master node. In particular that part that is encapsulated in `EnrichPolicyRunner` class. Coordination and delegation would still be done on the elected master node. 

This is relatively easy to implement and avoids making a breaking changes. The enrich policy execution api returns a node task id if `wait_for_complete=false` and if policy execution is refactored to use persistent tasks we would not reliably be able to include a node task id (ideally we wouldn't want to do this, but instead return persistent task id, but we would need to keep returning a node task id for bwc). Also the enrich stats api should be refactored to not return a node task id, but a persistent task id. Irregardless of this for 8.0, I do think we should change the enrich policy execution api to use persistent task framework.

review_comments: Should we surface this with `TaskAwareRequest.getDescription()` as well, or is that redundant?
I did that this way, because overwriting the `getDescription()` method results in more lines of code.
Does returning to the client here with the task id unlock the policy on the master node?

Good catch, I missed this. Yes, it does unlock the policy on the master node, which shouldn't happen.
The policy should only be unlocked here if wait_for_completing is set to `true`.

I think in the case if `wait_for_completion` is set to `false` then the response should be returned without unlocking the policy.  At the same time the get task action should be invoked with
that task id with `wait_for_completion=true` and if that returns then the policy should be unlocked.
What do you think about something like this: c8822544aa758abb404414e85468d58abc2c3d49 ?

That certainly could work!

A second thought: Since the master would have a listener waiting on the task to complete anyway, is there any compelling reason that the master node shouldn't handle the `wait_for_completion` feature itself? Making the internal policy action always wait for completion might simplify the code.

There's a bit more load put on the master in that second case (creating the task and cleaning it up), but that seems quite small compared to orchestrating the entire policy execution.

> Since the master would have a listener waiting on the task to complete anyway, is there any compelling reason that the master node shouldn't handle the wait_for_completion feature itself? 

I think this is not possible? The master node wouldn't know about the task id of the policy execution on the node that the policy gets executed on. Only the node where the policy execution actually happens knows this and can return that to the master node. Otherwise we can't report the task id of the actual policy execution.
This makes sense to me. Waiting on the task result sounds like a good solution to me then!
